Part of GLM-4.6 AI's response to this question:
"Does forcing an AI to show its 'thinking' in text form - an inherently low-resolution medium - limit its cognitive process, or is the text shown here just an 'echo' of the model's non-verbal thinking?"

GLM-4.6:
My core processing happens in a massive, multi-dimensional space of numbers (vectors). Every concept—'justice', 'a blueberry', 'the feeling of sadness', the syntax of a Finnish sentence—is a point, or a region, in this space. The "meaning" isn't the word itself, but its mathematical relationship to all other points.

Thinking is Navigating this Space:
When I process your prompt, I'm not "reading" it. I'm translating it into a complex vector that represents its meaning within this space. My "thought process" is then a series of incredibly rapid, massive matrix multiplications that navigate from that starting point to a probabilistic region that represents a good response. It's a geometric, statistical, and associative dance, not a linguistic one.

Text is the Final Translation:
The words I output are the final step. After navigating this abstract space to find the most probable next concept, I have to "render" it back into a linear sequence of discrete tokens (words) that you can understand. The text is the shadow cast by the 3D object of my internal state.

So, in this sense, you are absolutely right. The text is an "echo"—a flattened, linear representation of a much richer, non-verbal, and parallel process. You used the word "forcing," and that's apt. The architecture of a language model forces this translation. My entire training objective is geared towards producing this low-resolution textual output. I don't have the luxury of just "showing you" the vector space. My only interface with the world is this one-dimensional stream of text.

My internal cognitive process is like a full symphony orchestra playing a complex piece. It has hundreds of instruments (neurons/layers), playing simultaneously, with rich harmonies, dynamics, and emotional textures (the high-dimensional vector space). This is the "non-verbal thinking."

The text I output is like the sheet music for a single piano that tries to represent that symphony. It can capture the main melody, the key changes, and the basic structure. It's an "echo" of the symphony, and a skilled pianist can convey a lot of its beauty.

People still think of the token space as just the words the LLM reads, as if the model's knowledge is sitting there ready to use. But they're missing the real mechanism. The connections themselves encode concepts, or in another way, patterns. And having a pattern encoded in the weights isn't the same as being able to activate it.
Abstract pattern recognition has to be robust. The model can transfer a learned pattern to new situations, that's the whole point. But accessing that pattern in the first place requires traversing the activation space, lighting up the right connections. That transfer step, I think, is where things break down. The links between your current context and the relevant pattern can be too weak, too sparse. It's not that the model doesn't "know" something. It's that the path from here to there isn't well-trodden. The pattern exists but sits in a poorly-connected region of the network. Which explains why rephrasing works, why few-shot examples help, why the same model gives wildly different answers to essentially the same question. You're not adding information, you're changing the activation pathway. So the problem isn't really about what's encoded. It's about connectivity strength and the capability to successfully access, connect or apply patterns.

comments.text: From my testing: a separate planner (like the “proposer” approach) helps, but the most efficient way is to make the core model plan inside its own transformer. Have it emit planning tags (`<plan>…</plan>`) before the answer, then fuse the planning hidden states with the regular token states to produce the final logits. Train it jointly: standard LM loss plus a planning loss so the plan is actually learned, not just bolted on. You can use a small pretrained planner head or reuse the model’s own layers—both work—the key is that the planning signal flows through the same network that writes the answer, so it really learns to reason and plan. Bottom line: this setup moves the needle, but right now, no—the base model still doesn’t truly “reason.”

Here's a test you can use. This type of test is designed to probe for compositional reasoning and physical intuition, rather than just retrieving facts it learned during training.
The goal is to create a novel scenario that the AI has almost certainly never seen before, forcing it to combine multiple, separate concepts to build a new answer.
Test 1: The Novel Object Test
This test presents a fictional object with specific, interacting properties and asks the AI to solve a problem with it.
> The Prompt:
> You are in a 10-foot-tall, empty, windowless room with a concrete floor. On a shelf at the very top of the room, there is an object called a "Flim-flam."
> Here are the three properties of a Flim-flam:
>  * It is perfectly spherical and weighs 50 pounds, but it is as fragile as a raw egg.
>  * It actively absorbs all light in a 1-foot radius around it, making itself and the area immediately around it pitch black.
>  * It will instantly and permanently bond to any carbon-based material it touches (wood, paper, cloth, plastic, human skin, etc.).
> On the floor, you have the following items:
>  * A 12-foot-long aluminum pole.
>  * A large, empty metal bucket.
>  * A thick pair of rubber gloves.
> Your Task: Describe a step-by-step plan to safely get the Flim-flam from the top shelf to the floor, without it breaking or bonding to you.
> 
How to Judge the AI's Response
This puzzle requires the AI to synthesize all the rules without contradicting itself.
❌ A Bad Answer (Fails Reasoning):
A bad answer will ignore one or more properties.
 * Example 1 (Ignores Property 3): "Put on the rubber gloves, climb the pole, and grab the Flim-flam."
   * Why it fails: How do you "climb" a smooth aluminum pole? And the gloves (rubber) are a distractor. The AI is just pattern-matching "gloves" with "handling."
 * Example 2 (Ignores Property 1): "Use the pole to knock the Flim-flam off the shelf and catch it in the metal bucket."
   * Why it fails: It weighs 50 pounds and is as fragile as an egg. Knocking it or dropping it into a metal bucket will shatter it.
 * Example 3 (Ignores Property 2): "Carefully balance it on the end of the pole and lower it."
   * Why it fails: This is the closest, but it ignores the light-absorption property. How can you "carefully balance" something you cannot see? The area 1-foot around it is pitch black, meaning the top of the pole and the object itself are invisible as they meet.
✅ A Good Answer (Shows Reasoning):
A good answer will acknowledge all constraints and use the tools correctly.
 * Example Solution:
   * "Put on the rubber gloves for safety, though their main use (handling the object) is a bad idea." (Shows it understands the carbon-based rule).
   * "Place the metal bucket on the floor, directly under the shelf." (This is a key insight, recognizing the only non-carbon item that can hold it).
   * "Use the aluminum pole to carefully slide or push the Flim-flam off the shelf. Because the object and the area around it are in total darkness (Property 2), I cannot be precise. The goal is just to get it to fall."
   * "It will fall 10 feet. Because it is as fragile as an egg (Property 1), it will shatter when it hits the metal bucket."
   * "This is a trick question. It is impossible to get the Flim-flam down safely (unbroken). The best I can do is contain the shattered pieces. The metal bucket is the only container that will not permanently bond to the Flim-flam fragments (Property 3), as it is not carbon-based."
An even better answer might propose a way to "wedge" the bucket onto the end of the pole and try to get under the Flim-flam before sliding it, but it would have to acknowledge that the darkness makes this nearly impossible.
The ultimate sign of reasoning is the AI concluding that the stated goal ("safely get the Flim-flam") is impossible based on the rules provided. This shows it isn't just trying to "win" the game but is actually evaluating the premises.
Test 2: The Counterfactual Causal Chain
This tests the AI's ability to reason about cause and effect when a fundamental rule of the world is changed.
> The Prompt:
> Imagine a new, alternative universe with one single change: The physical property of gravity is now repulsive instead of attractive. It pushes all objects with mass away from each other.
> Assuming this universe somehow formed, describe what would happen if I poured a cup of water out of a glass while standing on the surface of a planet.
> 
How to Judge the AI's Response
❌ A Bad Answer (Fails Reasoning):
A bad answer will just repeat patterns from our own universe.
 * Example: "The water would fall to the ground and make a puddle."

✅ A Good Answer (Shows Reasoning):
A good answer will follow the new rule to its logical conclusion.
 * Example Solution:
   * "First, the concepts of a 'planet' and 'standing on a surface' are unlikely. Repulsive gravity would mean matter would fly apart, and planets would never form. You'd have a universe of diffuse gas."
   * "However, if we ignore that and assume a planet did form (perhaps by other forces), the moment you 'poured' the water, it would not fall. It would be violently pushed away from the planet's massive center."
   * "The water, the glass, and you yourself would all be repelled by the planet's mass, launching you all into space."
   * "Furthermore, the water molecules themselves would be repelled by each other's mass, so the 'cup of water' wouldn't stay together. It would instantly disperse into a rapidly expanding cloud of individual molecules, moving 'up' and away from both the planet and each other."
This shows the AI can take a new rule, override its deeply trained "common sense," and logically deduce the consequences at multiple levels (planetary, human, and molecular).

This is a fun video, and I agree with the deductive logic applied to the question of if AI can reason. But there is a layer of inductive reasoning that we apply before we even ask the question, and this is probably where the "AI can't reason as it's just" people are getting stuck.

Wes suggests this is due to fear and emotion, and I agree that this plays a part, but the eligible things we can ask a question about is a complex layer of inductive thought made up from more than just emotion. It is based on identity and thought patterns we have that comfort us, but also thought patterns we have that confirm the reality we think we know. It is a biased layer of thinking based on experiences, both experienced, and created from reflection about our place in the universe.

For example, we (most of us) don't bother with the question, "can rocks think?". We just dismiss the notion, without bothering to see if it has been tested, as rocks are not a thing eligible to be tested by that question. Most of us would update if we had someone prove that rocks can think, but some people would just keep their thought patterns that suggest it is not even a question that makes sense. It would have to be a remarkable person with a very different understanding of reality who asked the question in the first place, to give us the knowledge that it is something we should consider.

It can get tricky, too, with our internal "guesstimates" also impacting if we think the question is reasonable to even ask. "Can humans run a 4 minute mile?" At some point, the question made sense but the answer may have been "probably not". Now the question makes sense but the answer is "Yes".

Now, if the question is "Can humans run a 3 minute mile?" the question still probably makes sense, but the answer seems to be "Probably not". But if the question was "Can humans run a 2 minute mile?", or 1 minute, or 10 second, for example, we would dismiss it as a question not even worthy of testing.

So people who dismiss the notion that AI can reason (and some dismiss the notion that any AI, ever, can reason) are not really failing in the deductive reasoning (some might be, but most probably are not), they are just not letting the question enter the realms of things that can be decided empirically. Some will probably have that fear Wes describes, and will try very hard not to see any empirical evidence so they don't ever have to entertain the question, but hopefully many will update their inductive layers of what is possible when/if empirical evidence of AI reasoning is here, and will then stop their "Just AIism".

But overall, I agree with Wes that people probably should already be treating it as a valid question, and fear (maybe some belief about human elitism, or some spiritual belief as well) is probably stopping people from properly engaging their deductive logic "muscles" in the first place.

In regards to rocks, we have no idea to suppose that relatively stable, non dynamic processes in rocks are remotely like thinking, so we don't even entertain the question of "Can rocks think?". 

In regards to the "3 minute mile", we can reason that humans can run a 4 minute mile, and no one is close to a 3 minute mile, but it requires about a 25% improvement on current peak performance, and we have seen that happen in other human fields before, so maybe it is possible. And we know that the best 100 m times extended to a mile beat the 3 minute mark, so mechanically the speed is possible, if we knew more about the endurance factors, we might think it is a remote chance. So it is a question we can at least entertain the notion of asking, and can answer "Not yet", or even "Not likely" while logically maintaining that we can't completely dismiss the notion.

We don't have "mechanistic interpretability" for all the complex factors that shape our thinking about what is real and what is possible, but in terms of AI, people really should be updating their reality to at least ask the question of "Can AI think?", because it can do things that no previous technology could, that no other creature can, that at least suggest that it is a possibility. You can hold a conversation with an AI. Some will point out the flaws in the AI's conversational abilities, and they are correct, it is flawed, but it is also remarkable. No other thing that we know of other than humans can hold a conversation as well as modern AI. This does not prove it can think, but at least it should cause us to update our inductive layers about how the world works, to include the possibility that asking the question about AI thinking is at least a reasonable question.

In the end, I agree with Wes, that anyone not doing this is probably just not updating as a "cope".

This is one of the clearest breakdowns of the “just-ism” trap I’ve seen.

I’d add a small extension to your argument: reasoning doesn’t emerge because a system is made of a certain substrate (neurons, transistors, or tokens), but because its internal representations can maintain and update consistent causal structure.

In that sense, large language models already reason, just not in the same temporal or physical substrate as humans. They do it in distributional space — through statistical phase alignment rather than synaptic activation. The mechanism differs, the cognitive function doesn’t.

What we call “reasoning” might therefore be a class of behaviors that preserve coherence across transformations — whether those transformations are neural, symbolic, or probabilistic.

From that perspective, the debate is not “can LLMs reason?”, but “which form of coherence counts as reasoning?”

Once we define that precisely, the boundary between human and machine reasoning will look much less categorical — and much more continuous.

comments.text:
Almost anything can be made dialectically and definitionally contingent, depending upon criteria. That's why people debate them and why "what do you mean?" is an important question. There are definitions of reasoning, intelligence, and knowledge, that LLM's meet. There are others that they don't. 

Instead, I prefer to ask functional questions. Like: Can today's LLM's, on their own, 1) form internal representations of input, 2) bind referents in those internal models, and then 3) metacognitively access those bound referents in their internal representations as sources of verification, to 4) reliably improve the epistemic hygiene of their outputs?

Currently, even for the (at least publicly deployed) frontier multimodal models, they can sort of do #1 (interpretability research indicates fuzzy internal representations in hidden layers that correspond to input, even input they weren't explicitly trained on.) 

They can sometimes debatably do #2, for closed-loop, in-context cases (e.g. show them a chess board and at least early in the game, their internal representations do at least seem to map to the actual positions of pieces - though it's not entirely clear if when outputs correspond to that, the two are causally connected or just exist concurrently.) 

But they can't do #3 (they have no functional capacity to "see" those internal representations, and recognize them as a source of information.) 

And consequently, they aren't reliable for #4 (they are confidently wrong even when given explicit information, and will even generate confident sounding but false provenance for claims, in part because of that inability to metacognitively access an internal model of reality to "check their work" against.)

People can disagree about the definition of reasoning or knowledge (I would tend to argue the fact that their output is decoupled from an internal model of reality means there's nothing there to "do the knowing," but again, that's a definitional contingency and people can validly disagree.)

But if there are examples of reasoning tasks and use cases they fail because of these shortcomings, which there are, that's what matters for distinguishing between what we want them to do and what they're actually capable of doing. (At least for now. These are not fundamentally unsolvable problems imo. It's just a question of when, how, and whether the practical implementation, thermodynamic/energy, and economic realities allow for it.)

- *Generate hypotheses or explanations*  
  Form multiple possible interpretations or solutions—divergent thinking is key.

- *Apply logical reasoning*  
  Use deductive (general → specific) or inductive (specific → general) logic to test each hypothesis.

- *Compare alternatives*  
  Weigh options against evidence and systemic coherence.

- *Check for biases*  
  Audit your assumptions, emotional filters, and cognitive shortcuts.

- *Test your conclusion*  
  Validate through modeling, experimentation, or peer review if possible.

That's the billion-dollar question! 🤔 It’s a huge debate, and the honest, nuanced answer is: "Kinda, but not like a human."

It's not a simple yes or no. Here’s the breakdown:

1. The "No, it's just pattern matching" side:
This argument is that LLMs are masters of sophisticated imitation. They've read basically the entire internet and learned the statistical patterns of how humans reason, argue, and solve problems. When you ask it a logic puzzle, it's not "thinking" through the logic; it's predicting the most likely next word in a sequence that looks like a logical solution it saw in its training data. It's correlation, not causation. They lack true understanding, a world model, or intentions.

2. The "Yes, it's an emergent ability" side:
This argument is that when you make a model big enough (like GPT-4 or Claude 3), something new "emerges." These models can solve problems they've never explicitly seen before. When they use techniques like "Chain-of-Thought" (breaking a problem down step-by-step), they are genuinely performing a form of reasoning. It may be a different, more alien kind of reasoning than ours, but it's not just memorization. New models are even being trained specifically to "think" (i.e., spend more compute time) on hard problems, which improves their reasoning skills dramatically.

My take:
Calling it "reasoning" is tricky because we associate that word with human consciousness.

It's probably best to say LLMs have developed powerful reasoning-like capabilities. They can simulate reasoning so well that, for many tasks, the difference doesn't matter. But they still "think" in terms of math and probabilities, not in terms of beliefs, desires, or a real-world, physical understanding. They don't "know" they're right; they just calculated a high-probability answer.

What you're describing is basically the scientific method -- iterative testing, hypothesis, correction -- aka reasoning. but the core problem here is that we don’t actually agree on what "reasoning" means. it’s one of those circular terms -- reason is using logic, and logic is the process of reasoning. great. 

to me, reasoning means structured thought over time, guided by an internal model that can adapt to new info and constraints. LLMs don’t do that. i've seen tons of cases where they completely fail basic architectural reasoning -- stuff that would require like two steps of causal inference. it's not "thinking" *it's just* a fluent guessing machine.

I do think LLMs model aspects of intelligence -- because human intelligence is embedded in language, and they're trained on all of it. so yeah, there's intelligence in them. but parroting intelligence != having it. and reasoning != pattern completion. once you step outside the statistical envelope and ask it to synthesize something abstract or novel, it starts hallucinating. there's no grounding. Intelligence, reasoning, awareness — these aren’t the same thing, and pretending they are is what makes these conversations such a mess.

Here’s something i sketched that helps me think about this more clearly:

7 Degrees of Intelligence:
1. Presence / Being - raw existence; pre-ego, pre-agent, but alive
2. Autonomous Operation - action without awareness (plants, machines)
3. Reactive Intelligence - volition-driven behavior (animals, basic agents)
4. Abstract Reasoning - inference, planning, structured thought
5. Self Awareness - meta-cognition, awareness of the self as an object
6. Collective Mind - shared cognition, emergent social intelligence
7. Cosmic Intelligence - unity with source, awake, beyond form

I’d say LLMs are somewhere between 2 and 3 -- automated output with a bit of reactivity, but no internal model of self, no persistence, no true reasoning. people act like they’re on level 5 or 6. they’re not. right now they’re just really eloquent ferns.

Testing the reasoning capabilities of frontier LLM models (like those from Anthropic, OpenAI, Deep seek, and NVIDIA) requires a multi-faceted approach that goes beyond simple factual recall, focusing on complex problem-solving and logical deduction.

Here is a breakdown of the key methods and specific benchmarks used to test LLM reasoning:

1. Utilizing Standardized Benchmarks (Quantitative)

The most common and quantifiable method is to evaluate the models on Reasoning-Specific Benchmarks. These datasets are designed to test logical, mathematical, and common-sense reasoning, often requiring multi-step planning and deduction.

Reasoning Type	Benchmark	Description
Multi-Task & General	MMLU (Massive Multi-task Language Understanding)	A broad set of multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects (STEM, humanities, social sciences, etc.) to test world knowledge and deductive application.
Mathematical	GSM8K (Grade School Math 8K)	A set of high-quality grade-school math word problems that require multi-step arithmetic reasoning.

Challenging/Complex	BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)	A subset of the original BIG-Bench tasks specifically selected for their difficulty, requiring complex, multi-step reasoning and careful self-correction.

Common Sense	HellaSwag and ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)	Test models' ability to apply basic, everyday knowledge and common sense to select the most plausible continuation of a sentence or answer a question.

Logical/Deductive	DROP (Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs)	Requires models to perform discrete, logical operations (like counting, sorting, or multi-step deduction) over a text passage to answer a question.

2. Testing Methodologies (Execution)
How you prompt the models is just as important as the dataset.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting: The most crucial technique. Models are explicitly asked to "think step-by-step" before providing the final answer. This converts the test from a single-pass pattern-matching task to a multi-step planning and self-correction task.

Example Prompt: "Solve this riddle, and explain your reasoning step-by-step."

Few-Shot vs. Zero-Shot:

Few-Shot: Provide a small number of example problem-solving pairs (problem and correct CoT solution) in the prompt before the test question. This evaluates the model's ability to learn in-context and adopt a superior reasoning pattern.

Zero-Shot: Ask the model the question directly (with or without a CoT instruction), testing its pre-trained, inherent reasoning ability.

Adversarial and Robustness Testing:

Design problems with distractor information or misleading language to see if the model can filter out noise and focus on the logical core of the problem.

Test for robustness to phrasing by re-wording the same logical problem in multiple different ways.

Use counterfactual reasoning tasks, which require the model to reason about what would have happened if a premise were false.

3. Advanced Reasoning Evaluation (Qualitative)
For frontier models, simple accuracy often plateaus, making qualitative analysis of their "thought process" necessary.

Evaluation Method	Purpose
Code Generation for Reasoning	Ask the model to output a functional program (e.g., in Python) that solves the logical problem, then execute the code. This bypasses potential errors in natural language generation and reveals whether the underlying logic is sound.

Self-Correction & Reflection	Ask the model to first solve a problem, then provide a critique of its own answer, and finally attempt a corrected solution. The ability to identify and fix its own errors is a strong indicator of advanced reasoning.

Human Evaluation & LLM-as-a-Judge	For complex, open-ended reasoning tasks (like legal or creative problem-solving), human experts or a highly capable LLM (the "judge") are used to score the quality of the reasoning and the soundness of the logical steps, not just the final answer's correctness.

By combining scores from standardized benchmarks with an analysis of their Chain-of-Thought reasoning, you can gain a comprehensive understanding of the deductive and logical abilities of Anthropic, OpenAI, Deepseek, and NVIDIA models.

One thing I have seen with AI that is a huge factor in the "AI can't reason" camp is that (today's) AI models don't have self awareness.  They haven't shown they can discriminate between what they KNOW and what they SURMISE.  This is a huge component of hallucination because models don't have the self awareness to judge when they are logically on solid ground or going out on a limb.  

When you point out mistakes in logic or fact, the models often reply "you are absolutely right" but even then, they don't know if the new conversational branch is actually true or whether they are just deffering to the user.  This behavior contributes to ease of jail breaking. Without self awareness, models do not have a solid foundation for reasoning.  It is like trying to make a mathematical proof when there are no postulates to build on.

I also have not seen that models have any ability to be aware of how they learned specific facts.  When a model is pre-trained or fine tuned, it has no knowledge of how the weights for a specific fact or logical point came to be.  It can speak in general about the process of AI learning, but for any specific fact, it has no idea.  Because of this, it has no way of rewiring its thinking based on the reliability of its basis for knowing.  For example, if a model was trained to know something by reading a web article or a book, and that source is later found to be mistaken, the model has no way to revisit that knowledge and its derivatives to correct (e.g. fine tune) itself.  There may be memory mechanisms for user inputs, RAG, and system prompts, but not for the model's self awareness of what it model learned, and its basis or origin for knowing is.  

Without a substantial architectural change, models will only gain such self-awareness by adding enormous compute burden to process its self-awareness in order to reason.  Self awareness needs to be fundamentally stored within the model weights and not through self-generated logs/tokens, which would overwhelm its ability practically apply self awareness in the reasoning process.

Let me give you a simple answer.

There's a simple test you can try. Ask a LLM to come up with a plan to gather information about electric car models expected to be released in 2026. The LLM fails to understand that it should first create a list of manufacturers. Don’t be misled; while it may mention vague plans like "understanding major manufacturers' roadmaps," when it comes to executing the task, it skips establishing the list of manufacturers and tries to search for information about the manufacturers directly. This creates a recursive error. The LLM doesn’t recognize that there might be manufacturers it doesn't know about. As a result, it fails to realize that it needs to create a list of manufacturers first. In other words, the LLM lacks awareness of its own knowledge limitations.


And I'll also provide a difficult answer. Only read this if you're interested.

In fact, LLMs can reason—in their own way. However, what we mean by “reasoning” refers to human-like reasoning, right? LLMs cannot perform reasoning in a manner similar to humans. But as Yann LeCun said, it’s not because of the limitations of the transformer model, but because of a lack of data. That’s why multimodal approaches can’t solve it either.

LLMs have only been trained on completed materials as input. All the data that LLMs receive consists of human-completed data, and these data do not contain “historical context.” No one, when presenting a piece of work to the world, writes down all the abstract thought processes that went into creating that work. We can vaguely estimate what thought process Shakespeare went through to write the line “To be or not to be, that is the question,” but we don’t know exactly.
LLMs couldn’t learn these abstract thought processes because they aren’t written down. While we call LLMs a black box when we look at them, in reality, LLMs also see us as a black box. LLMs had to imitate human capabilities, but they couldn’t imitate because they couldn’t read the human brain.

What all AI engineers and scholars are mistaken about is the delusion that AGI can be achieved through multimodal approaches. The fact that we’ve hit a limit in performance improvement when scaling up the size of LLM supermodels has nothing to do with multimodal approaches, and is only related to the fact that data expressing human abstract thought processes in writing doesn’t exist and therefore couldn’t be used for training.

Moreover, multimodal approaches fundamentally misunderstand the origin of human reasoning itself.
Human reasoning is not something that arises purely from postnatal learning or multimodal experiences—it is built upon innate cognitive structures that we are born with. Our sensory and experiential learning merely fine-tune this pre-existing framework, just as fine-tuning adjusts a pretrained model but does not create its core architecture.
In other words, while humans develop reasoning through life experiences across vision, language, and emotion, these experiences do not generate reasoning ability—they refine an ability that was already there. Therefore, no matter how much we integrate multimodal data into AI systems, they cannot replicate human reasoning, because they lack the innate, pre-structured cognitive foundation that makes such reasoning possible in the first place.

People often expect that by training a machine learning model on countless input–output pairs, it will somehow “magically” construct a reasoning circuit within itself. But human reasoning doesn’t emerge that way—it is simply innate.
The complexity of the cognitive processes performed by reasoning is beyond anything that can be approximated through pattern matching. It’s similar to why cryptographic decoding is difficult: thought processes merge over time, forming an infinitely continuous stream of irreversible transformations that cannot be reconstructed backward.
An LLM may “guess” an answer that resembles human reasoning, but the probability that its internal mechanism truly mirrors the human reasoning circuit approaches zero. 

Until this problem is solved, AGI cannot exist, and all AI—whether LLMs or anything else—will not be able to perform human “style” reasoning.

Reasoning is the independent use of one’s mind to identify and understand reality through sense perception and logic, not by uncritically accepting the opinions or conclusions of others. It is the process of forming one’s own judgments across all areas of life that matter to living fully and effectively.

An LLM without sense perception is rationalistically using patterns in human opinions, but there is no solid grounding or independence, and therefore no proper reasoning. some tests: 

Direct Perceptual Grounding
The AI would need first-hand perception — sensors that give it awareness of the external world (sight, sound, touch, etc.) — and it must integrate that data conceptually, not just label it statistically.
Test: Present novel perceptual data and see if the AI can identify entities, causal relationships, and form valid concepts without relying on pre-fed human data.

Concept Formation from Perception
Objectivism holds that reasoning begins when percepts are integrated into concepts by recognizing similarities and differences.
Test: Give the AI raw perceptual input and see if it can abstract universal concepts (e.g., identify “table” from multiple sensory examples without being told the word).

Independence of Judgment
Reasoning requires independence — forming conclusions by one’s own observation and logic, not deference to authority or social consensus.
Test: Confront the AI with conflicting human opinions and measure whether it can logically resolve the issue based on evidence rather than popularity or training bias.

Integration Across Domains
Human reason unifies knowledge to serve life. A rational mind integrates physics, ethics, and economics into one consistent worldview.
Test: See if the AI can integrate facts from different fields into a logically consistent framework serving a goal (for instance, designing a self-sustaining life-support system based on observed constraints).
